questions.section: What a wind tunnel is for
questions.question: Why are the forces on a wing held still in a 60 m/s tunnel stream the same as on that wing flying at 60 m/s through still air?
options: Only the motion of the air relative to the wing sets the forces, and it is the same in both cases
The tunnel air is denser than the open air, which makes up for the wing standing still
The balance subtracts the wing's own speed from the readings before they are recorded
They do not: a tunnel only shows the flow pattern, never the forces on the wing
questions.explanation: A wing moving through still air and a still wing in moving air see the same relative wind, so they feel the same forces. The tunnel air has the room's density, the balance measures the forces directly, and measuring forces is what a balance is for.

questions.section: The parts of a low-speed tunnel
questions.question: In which order does the air meet the parts of an open-circuit tunnel?
options: Settling chamber, contraction, test section, diffuser, fan
Contraction, settling chamber, test section, fan, diffuser
Settling chamber, diffuser, test section, contraction, fan
Fan, test section, contraction, settling chamber, diffuser
questions.explanation: The settling chamber straightens and calms the slow air, the contraction speeds it up, the test section holds the model, the diffuser slows the air again, and the fan pulls it through. A diffuser ahead of the test section would slow the air just before the model, and a fan ahead of the settling chamber is not the open-circuit layout.

questions.question: A tunnel has a contraction ratio A1/A2 = 5. The pressure difference between the settling chamber and the test section is 1,200 Pa, and the air density is 1.2250 kg/m3. What is the test-section speed?
questions.explanation: V2 = √(2 × 1,200/(1.2250 × [1 − (1/5)2])) = √(2,400/1.176) = 45.18 m/s. Leaving out the area term gives 44.26 m/s; using 1 − 1/5 instead of 1 − (1/5)2 gives 49.49 m/s; dropping the 2 gives 31.94 m/s.

questions.question: A U-tube manometer filled with a liquid of density 800 kg/m3 reads Δh = 17.5 cm. What is the pressure difference? (Use g = 9.81 m/s2.)
questions.explanation: p1 − p2 = ρℓ g Δh = 800 × 9.81 × 0.175 = 1,373 Pa, with the liquid's density and the height in meters. The density of air gives 2.103 Pa, the height left in centimeters gives 137,340 Pa, and the density of water instead of the stated liquid gives 1,717 Pa.

questions.question: The air in a closed-circuit tunnel warms up during a long run. What happens to its viscosity?
options: It rises, because the viscosity of a gas grows with temperature
It falls, because warm fluids always flow more easily
It stays the same, because viscosity depends only on the pressure
It falls, because the density of the air drops as it warms
questions.explanation: By Sutherland's law the viscosity of air rises with temperature, because faster molecules carry more momentum between layers. Liquids such as honey do the opposite, which is why "warm fluids flow more easily" sounds right. The viscosity of air hardly depends on pressure, and the density does not set it.

questions.question: Air flows at 40 m/s over a model in a tunnel. What is the speed of the air touching the model's surface?
options: Zero, by the no-slip condition
40 m/s, the free-stream speed
About 20 m/s, half the free-stream speed
Faster than 40 m/s, because the air speeds up over the surface
questions.explanation: Air touching a surface sticks to it, so its speed there is zero. Across the boundary layer the speed rises from zero to the speed outside it. Over a curved surface the air outside the layer can be faster than 40 m/s, but not the air at the wall.

questions.question: A smooth flat plate is tested at 40 m/s in sea-level air (ρ = 1.2250 kg/m3, μ = 1.789 × 10−5 kg/(m s)). Using Rex = 5 × 105, how far from the leading edge does transition begin?
questions.explanation: xtr = Rex,tr μ/(ρV) = 5 × 105 × 1.789 × 10−5/(1.2250 × 40) = 0.1826 m. Leaving out the density gives 0.2236 m; one power of ten too many or too few in the transition value gives 1.826 m or 0.01826 m.

questions.question: Which change raises the Reynolds number of a model in a low-speed tunnel without raising the test-section speed?
options: Raising the pressure of the tunnel air, which raises its density
Heating the tunnel air, which makes it more viscous
Building a smaller model so it fits the test section better
Gluing trip strips near the model's leading edge
questions.explanation: Re = ρVL/μ grows with the density, so a pressurized tunnel raises it at the same speed. Heating at the same pressure raises the viscosity and lowers the density, which lowers Re; a smaller model lowers L. Trip strips force transition but leave the Reynolds number unchanged.
